# What the James Webb Space Telescope Has Found So Far

When you look at a distant galaxy, you're seeing light that left it long ago, so the picture is old. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST, or Webb) sees farther back in time than any telescope before it. Some of what it found was so unexpected that astronomers had to rethink parts of their theories about the early universe.

## A telescope built to see heat

Webb launched in December 2021 and started sending back data that genuinely surprised even the scientists who built it.<Cite refs={["turn0search0"]}/> It's different from older telescopes because it mostly sees <KeyTerm term="infrared" definition="Light with longer wavelengths than red light. Our eyes can't see it, but we feel it as heat."/> light.

Infrared light gives Webb two advantages:

1. **It sees through dust.** Clouds of space dust block ordinary light, but infrared light passes through those clouds easily.<Cite refs={["turn0search0"]}/> That lets Webb photograph baby stars hidden inside them.
2. **It sees the oldest light.** As the universe expands, light traveling through it gets stretched. This stretching is called <KeyTerm term="redshift" definition="How much light has been stretched to longer, redder wavelengths by the expansion of the universe. Higher redshift means farther away and further back in time."/>. The higher the redshift, the farther the object is.<Cite refs={["turn0search1"]}/> Light from the very first galaxies has been stretched so much that it now reaches us as infrared, and Webb was designed to catch exactly that.

<CompareToggle title="Hubble vs. Webb" left={{"label":"Hubble (1990)","points":["Sees mostly visible and ultraviolet light","Mirror 2.4 m wide","Dust clouds block much of its view","Can see back to about 400 million years after the Big Bang"]}} right={{"label":"Webb (2021)","points":["Sees mostly infrared light","Gold-coated mirror 6.5 m wide","Sees through dust to stars still forming","Can see back to about 280 million years after the Big Bang"]}}/>

constants.0: What the James Webb Space Telescope Has Found So Far
constants.1: When you look at a distant galaxy, you're seeing light that left it long ago, so the picture is old. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST, or Webb) sees farther back in time than any telescope before it. Some of what it found was so unexpected that astronomers had to rethink parts of their theories about the early universe.
constants.2: A telescope built to see heat

constants.9: Infrared light gives Webb two advantages:
constants.11: Clouds of space dust block ordinary light, but infrared light passes through those clouds easily.
constants.14: That lets Webb photograph baby stars hidden inside them.
constants.16: As the universe expands, light traveling through it gets stretched. This stretching is called
constants.18: . The higher the redshift, the farther the object is.
constants.21: Light from the very first galaxies has been stretched so much that it now reaches us as infrared, and Webb was designed to catch exactly that.
constants.24: Webb keeps breaking its own distance record.
constants.25: The current record holder is a galaxy called MoM-z14. We see it as it was only 280 million years after the Big Bang.
constants.28: At that point the universe was about 2% of its current age.
constants.31: Think of the universe's age as one day. MoM-z14 comes from the first half hour, just after midnight.
constants.32: Back in 2022, Hubble held the record with a galaxy called GN-z11.
constants.35: By 2025, that galaxy wasn't even in the top 10.
constants.38: Here's the surprise. Scientists expected early galaxies to be small and dim. Instead, Webb found more bright, ancient galaxies than scientists expected.
constants.41: MoM-z14 is a good example. It is surprisingly bright and chemically "grown-up" for something so young.
constants.46: Big, bright galaxies this early means stars formed faster than we thought. Scientists are now working out how.
constants.48: Webb also found something nobody asked for.
constants.49: Deep in early space, it spotted lots of tiny, very red objects. Researchers began calling them Little Red Dots.
constants.52: They are not rare. On average, there's about one in every deep Webb image.
constants.55: So what are they? Nobody is fully sure yet. The leading idea is that they are young
constants.58: New computer simulations in 2026 suggest the dots are fast-growing black holes from the early universe.
constants.61: Another team had a different idea. They suggested the dots may be gigantic, short-lived stars.
constants.64: Both ideas point to the same big question: how did huge black holes appear so early?
constants.66: Reading the air of faraway planets
constants.69: . It can even tell what their air is made of.
constants.70: One famous case is a planet called WASP-39 b. It's a hot gas giant, about as heavy as Saturn.
constants.73: It orbits a Sun-like star 700 light-years away.
constants.76: In 2022, Webb found the first clear evidence of carbon dioxide in the air of a planet outside our solar system.
constants.79: It also found more. It was the first time sulfur dioxide was detected on an exoplanet too.
constants.82: How does Webb do it without even taking a photo of the planet? Step through it below.
constants.84: This success suggests Webb may one day measure carbon dioxide on smaller, rocky planets too.
constants.89: You can now explain three of Webb's biggest discoveries in plain words. Nice work!

106.label: Why do the dots look red?
106.content: Their light has traveled so far that it got stretched (redshifted). Stretched light looks redder.

106.label: Are scientists sure what they are?
106.content: Not yet. Fast-growing black holes are the top idea, but the debate is still open.

constants.108: Planets that orbit stars other than our Sun.

109.text: Every 4 days, WASP-39 b crosses in front of its star, as seen from Earth.
109.label: 1. The planet passes in front

109.text: Some starlight passes through the planet's thin layer of air on its way to us.
109.label: 2. Starlight shines through the air

109.text: Each gas soaks up its own colors of light. Carbon dioxide takes certain infrared colors.
109.label: 3. Gases steal some colors

109.text: Webb splits the light into a rainbow. Dips in the rainbow show which colors are missing.
109.label: 4. Webb spots the missing colors

109.text: The missing colors match carbon dioxide's pattern. So the planet's air contains carbon dioxide.
109.label: 5. Match the fingerprint

constants.110: Worked example: tasting WASP-39 b's air

111.hint: Think about starlight passing through the air.
111.explanation: Each gas absorbs its own colors. The missing colors matched carbon dioxide.

# What the James Webb Space Telescope Has Found So Far

When you look at a distant galaxy, you're seeing light that left it long ago, so the picture is old. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST, or Webb) sees farther back in time than any telescope before it. Some of what it found was so unexpected that astronomers had to rethink parts of their theories about the early universe.

## A telescope built to see heat

Webb launched in December 2021 and started sending back data that genuinely surprised even the scientists who built it. It's different from older telescopes because it mostly sees **infrared** (Light with longer wavelengths than red light. Our eyes can't see it, but we feel it as heat.) light.

Infrared light gives Webb two advantages:

1. **It sees through dust.** Clouds of space dust block ordinary light, but infrared light passes through those clouds easily. That lets Webb photograph baby stars hidden inside them.
2. **It sees the oldest light.** As the universe expands, light traveling through it gets stretched. This stretching is called **redshift** (How much light has been stretched to longer, redder wavelengths by the expansion of the universe. Higher redshift means farther away and further back in time.). The higher the redshift, the farther the object is. Light from the very first galaxies has been stretched so much that it now reaches us as infrared, and Webb was designed to catch exactly that.

**Hubble vs. Webb**

- **Hubble (1990)**: Sees mostly visible and ultraviolet light; Mirror 2.4 m wide; Dust clouds block much of its view; Can see back to about 400 million years after the Big Bang
- **Webb (2021)**: Sees mostly infrared light; Gold-coated mirror 6.5 m wide; Sees through dust to stars still forming; Can see back to about 280 million years after the Big Bang

## The oldest galaxies ever seen

Webb keeps breaking its own distance record.

The current record holder is a galaxy called MoM-z14. We see it as it was only 280 million years after the Big Bang. At that point the universe was about 2% of its current age.

Think of the universe's age as one day. MoM-z14 comes from the first half hour, just after midnight.

Back in 2022, Hubble held the record with a galaxy called GN-z11. By 2025, that galaxy wasn't even in the top 10.

Here's the surprise. Scientists expected early galaxies to be small and dim. Instead, Webb found more bright, ancient galaxies than scientists expected. MoM-z14 is a good example. It is surprisingly bright and chemically "grown-up" for something so young.

**How soon after the Big Bang? (lower = older light)**

- **GN-z11 (Hubble record)** (400 million years)
- **JADES-GS-z14-0 (Webb)** (290 million years)
- **MoM-z14 (Webb)** (280 million years)

**Why this matters** Big, bright galaxies this early means stars formed faster than we thought. Scientists are now working out how.

## Mystery "little red dots"

Webb also found something nobody asked for.

Deep in early space, it spotted lots of tiny, very red objects. Researchers began calling them Little Red Dots. They are not rare. On average, there's about one in every deep Webb image.

So what are they? Nobody is fully sure yet. The leading idea is that they are young **black holes** (Places where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.), growing very fast.

New computer simulations in 2026 suggest the dots are fast-growing black holes from the early universe. Another team had a different idea. They suggested the dots may be gigantic, short-lived stars.

Both ideas point to the same big question: how did huge black holes appear so early?

**Predict, then check**

- **Why do the dots look red?**: Their light has traveled so far that it got stretched (redshifted). Stretched light looks redder.
- **Are scientists sure what they are?**: Not yet. Fast-growing black holes are the top idea, but the debate is still open.

## Reading the air of faraway planets

Webb can also study **exoplanets** (Planets that orbit stars other than our Sun.). It can even tell what their air is made of.

One famous case is a planet called WASP-39 b. It's a hot gas giant, about as heavy as Saturn. It orbits a Sun-like star 700 light-years away.

In 2022, Webb found the first clear evidence of carbon dioxide in the air of a planet outside our solar system. It also found more. It was the first time sulfur dioxide was detected on an exoplanet too.

How does Webb do it without even taking a photo of the planet? Step through it below.

**Worked example: tasting WASP-39 b's air**

- **1. The planet passes in front**: Every 4 days, WASP-39 b crosses in front of its star, as seen from Earth.
- **2. Starlight shines through the air**: Some starlight passes through the planet's thin layer of air on its way to us.
- **3. Gases steal some colors**: Each gas soaks up its own colors of light. Carbon dioxide takes certain infrared colors.
- **4. Webb spots the missing colors**: Webb splits the light into a rainbow. Dips in the rainbow show which colors are missing.
- **5. Match the fingerprint**: The missing colors match carbon dioxide's pattern. So the planet's air contains carbon dioxide.

This success suggests Webb may one day measure carbon dioxide on smaller, rocky planets too.

## Check your understanding

**Check your understanding**

1. Why does Webb mostly use infrared light?
- Infrared light is brighter than visible light
- Light from the earliest galaxies has been stretched into infrared
- Infrared only comes from nearby stars
2. Webb found fewer bright early galaxies than scientists expected.
- True
- False
3. How did Webb find carbon dioxide on WASP-39 b?
- It took a close-up photo of the planet's clouds
- It checked which colors of starlight went missing after passing through the planet's air
- It measured how hot the planet was

You can now explain three of Webb's biggest discoveries in plain words. Nice work!
